parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin ā fortiōrī.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā posteriōrī (literally “from what follows”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”).
From a- + balanza (“balance”) + -ar, the second element from Medieval Latin bilantia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin abyssālis.

parole.significato: pumpkin, squash (any vegetable belonging to the family Cucurbitaceae)
parole.testo: From Hispanic Medieval Latin apopores, apoperes, of unknown origin.
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin advocātia, from Latin advocātus (“attorney”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin abrotanum, from Latin abrotonum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin acadēmicus, from Ancient Greek ἀκαδημικός (akadēmikós).

parole.significato: to accentuate (to pronounce with vocal stress)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin accentuāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin actitūdō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin āctuāre (“actuate”), from Latin āctus, perfect passive participle of agō (“do, act”).
Inherited from Old Spanish acuçia (c. 1240), borrowed from Medieval Latin acūtia.
From acucia (“diligence, ardent desire”) + -ar, semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin acūtiēs (“sharpness”), from Latin acūtus. Possibly related to crucial.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin adhaesīvus, from Latin adhaereō (supine adhaesum).

From a + Dios, literally “to God”, from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”); compare Aragonese, Asturian, and Extremaduran adiós, Catalan adeu, Dutch aju, ajuus, Low German atjüs, English, French, and Occitan adieu, Galician and Portuguese adeus, German tschüss, Greek αντίο (antío), Italian addio, Mal
Borrowed from Medieval Latin admissibilis, which was based on Old French admissible, or formed from the root of Latin admissus with the suffix -ible.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin affīliāre (“to adopt as a son”). Doublet of ahijar.
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin afflūxus.
From Medieval Latin alberga, from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin alcanna, from Arabic الحِنَّاء (al-ḥinnāʔ). Doublet of alheña.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin algorismus, from Arabic الخَوَارِزْمِيّ (al-ḵawārizmiyy). Influenced by ritmo.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin allōdium, from Frankish *allaaud.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient”), from μαλάσσω (malássō, “to soften”), from μαλακός (malakós, “soft”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ambidexter, from Latin ambi- + dexter.

parole.significato: ambo (a raised platform in certain churches)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ambōnem, from Ancient Greek ἄμβων (ámbōn).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ampullosus, from Latin ampulla.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”). Doublet of almendra and mandorla.

parole.significato: anarchy (the state of a society being without authorities)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin anarchia, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Anglicānus, suggested in the Magna Carta by Anglicana ecclesia (“the English church”), from Latin Anglicus, from Angli, Anglus (“an Englishman”).
From Medieval Latin amineus (“white”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin annichilāre, present active infinitive of annichilō, from Late Latin annihilāre (“to reduce to nothing”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin anormālis, variant of anormalus, corruption of anōmalus by confusion with norma (“norm, standard”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin antichresis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίχρησις (antíkhrēsis), from ἀντί (antí) + χρῆσις (khrêsis), from χράω (khráō).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Antōnīniānus, a name invented in modern times, as the Roman name is not known.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “verse response”), from ἀντίφωνος (antíphōnos, “responsive”), from ἀντί (antí, “against, in return”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aperitivus, from Late Latin apertivus, from Latin aperiō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin apocopāre (“to cut off”).

parole.significato: to fork out, shell out (to pay, usually reluctantly)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps derived from Medieval Latin apochāre (“to pay as tax”); compare Leonese apochar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin apothegma, from Ancient Greek ἀπόφθεγμα (apóphthegma).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aptitūdinem.
From the feminine past participle of armar, corresponding to Medieval Latin armāta, from the feminine perfect passive participle of Latin armāre, from arma (“arms”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin armistitium, from Latin arma (“weapons”) and statio (“immobility”) (compare solstitium). Cognate to French armistice, French armistice, Italian armistizio, Portuguese armistício, Catalan armistici.

parole.significato: astrolabe (an astronomical and navigational instrument for gauging the altitude of the Sun and stars)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin astrolabium, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολάβος (astrolábos, “star-taking”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin auctorizāre.

parole.significato: authentic, real, true (conforming to reality and therefore worthy of trust)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós, “original, genuine, principal”), from αὐθέντης (authéntēs, “one acting by his own authority, perpetrator, ruler”), from αὐτός (autós, “self”).
From Medieval Latin avunculāris, from Classical Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -āris (“-ar”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bacina. Compare Old French bacin.
Inherited from Old Spanish bacin (c. 1250), from Medieval Latin bacinus, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum (“basin, wide bowl”).

parole.significato: balance, scale (device used to measure weight)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin balantia, from Latin bilanx. Compare English balance.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bahobab, from Arabic أَبُو حِبَاب (ʔabū ḥibāb, “father of many seeds”), from أَبُو (ʔabū, “father”) + حَبّ (ḥabb, “seed”).

Variant of dialectal berniz, from Medieval Latin vernicem (“sandarac, resin”) from veronicem, from Byzantine Greek [Term?], from Ancient Greek βερενίκιον (bereníkion, “soda”), βερονίκιον (beroníkion), from Βερενίκη (Bereníkē). Cognate with English varnish.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin beātificātiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin beātificāre (“to bless”). By surface analysis, beato + -ificar.
Derived from Medieval Latin be molle (“B-flat”, literally “soft B”). By surface analysis, be + mole.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium, from Latin bēstia.
Inherited from Old Spanish bote, from Medieval Latin buccus, of Germanic origin, see also German Bock.

parole.significato: a muzzle; device to stop an animal from biting
parole.testo: From bozo (“muzzle”) + -al, from Medieval Latin *buccĕus (“relating or belonging to the mouth”). See bucca for more.

parole.significato: down, peach fuzz (soft hair on the upper lip)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *buccĕus (“relating or belonging to the mouth”). See bucca for more.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin brūtālis (“savage, stupid”), from brūtus (“dull, stupid”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin būbōnēs (“buboes”), from Ancient Greek βουβών (boubṓn, “groin, swelling in the groin”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin bulla (“seal, sealed document; bull”), from Latin bulla (“swollen object”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“swelling”) or *bʰel- (“to blow, to swell up”). Doublet of bola and bolla.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin calamina, q.v.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin calefactorium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin quālificātiōnem, from quālificō.
From Medieval Latin quālificāre, from quālis + -ficō. Cognate with English qualify.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin camahutus, alternative form of camaeus (“jewellery carved in relief”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin camarārius (Late Latin camerārius (“chamberlain”)), related to cámara (“room”). Compare Catalan cambrer and Italian cameriere.
Inherited from Old Spanish camino, from Medieval Latin cammīnus, from Gaulish. Cognate with Portuguese caminho, Italian cammino or French chemin.

Inherited from Old Spanish candelero, a semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin candēlārius. Analyzable as candela (“candle”) + -ero. Compare Portuguese candeeiro, Catalan candeler, French chandelier, Italian candelaio.
Medieval Latin capiro, from cappa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin charactērizō, from Ancient Greek χαρακτηρίζω (kharaktērízō), from χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin chartulārium, chartularius, from Latin chartula.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin zedoārium, from Arabic جَدْوَار (jadwār), from Persian ژدوار (žadvâr).

parole.significato: celestial, heavenly (of or relating to heaven as the place where deities (or the Christian God), spiritual beings, etc.…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin caelestiālis, from Latin caelestis, based on caelum (“sky, heaven”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin cenit, from Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”), from the fuller form سَمْت اَلرَّأْس (samt ar-raʔs, “direction of the head”). The -ni- for -m- is sometimes thought to be due to a misreading of the three strokes, which is plausible, though it could be a mere phonetic
Borrowed from Medieval Latin centaurēa.
From Medieval Latin ceromantia, from Ancient Greek κηρός (kērós, “wax”) + -mancia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin claustrālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin claustrum (“portion of monastery closed off to laity”), from Latin claustrum (“place shut in, bar, bolt, enclosure”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coalitiōnem, from Latin coalitus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin collector, from Latin collectus.

parole.significato: jump rope (the rope itself, not the game)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cumba (“valley”), borrowed from Gaulish *cumba, from Proto-Celtic *kumbā. According to Coromines, the term likely passed through Asturleonese or Mozarabic because of the retention of Latin /mb/, with the expected native outcome being *coma. However, this is not universally agreed
Borrowed from Medieval Latin compatibilis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin concernere (“to distinguish, have respect to”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- + cernō (“distinguish”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin conditiōnālis (“conditional”), from conditiō (“condition”). Cognate with English conditional.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre.

parole.significato: conjunctiva (membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin conjūnctīva (“serving to connect, connective”, feminine), ellipsis of membrāna conjūnctīva (literally “conjunctive membrane”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotāre (“to mark in addition”), from Latin con- (“together, with”) + noto (“to note”); equivalent to con- + notar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin coōrdināre (“arrange together”), from Latin co- (“together”) + ōrdinō (“to arrange”).
From Medieval Latin cūpella (probably via Italian coppella), diminutive of Latin cūpa (“cask”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin correlātiōnem.

parole.significato: to correspond to (be similar in character, quantity, quality, origin, structure, function etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin correspondēre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin coxālis, from Latin coxa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin crēdibilitātem, from Latin credibilis.

From creer + -encia or a semi-learned modification of the Old Spanish creença < Medieval Latin or Late Latin crēdentia, from Latin crēdēns. Compare the doublet credencia. Cognates include English credence, French croyance, French créance, Italian credenza, Portuguese crença, Romanian credință.
Derived from Medieval Latin crīminālitātem.
From Medieval Latin criterium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin crānium, from Ancient Greek κρανίον (kraníon).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin quaternus, from Latin quaternī (“four each”), in the sense of quarto sheets.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin quālificātiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin culmināre, from Latin culmen.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cultīvāre (“to till, cultivate”), from cultīvus (“tilled”), from Latin cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“to till, cultivate”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin curativus. By surface analysis, curar + -t- + -ivo.
From cura + -ato (having cura the sense of priest), or borrowed from Medieval Latin cūrātus, with the sense of "hability to heal souls". Doublet of the inherited curado.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cursivus, from Latin cursus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cabbala, from Hebrew קַבָּלָה (kabalá, “Jewish mysticism”, literally “something received”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cedula, diminutive form of scheda.
From Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from dē- + canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”), equivalent to Spanish de- + canto (“edge”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin decīsīvus. Compare French décisif.

parole.significato: defective (having one or more defects), faulty, flawed
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēfectuōsus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēfēnsīvus.

parole.significato: delphinal (of or relating to a dauphin)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin delphinālis, from delphīnus + -ālis. By surface analysis, delfín + -al.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dentālis, from Latin dēns (“a tooth”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin depauperare (“to impoverish”), from Latin de- + pauperare (“to impoverish”), from pauper (“poor”). Cognate with Italian depauperare, English depauperate.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēpūrāre, from pūrus (“pure”).
From de- + early Medieval Latin rocca (“boulder”), whence English rock.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēscendentia, from Latin dēscendēns. Compare Italian discendenza.

parole.significato: ending or termination that is attached to a word stem
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dēsinentia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēspectīvus (“disrespectful”). Cognate with English despised.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin devolutiōnem, from Latin devolvō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diametrālis. By surface analysis, diámetro (“diameter”) + -al.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dictiōnārium (“dictionary”), from Latin dictiō + -ārium, or possibly from older Latin dictiōnārius.

parole.significato: diet (a council or assembly of leaders)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dieta (“day's work, wages”) and also "meeting of councilors", from Latin diaeta (“prescribed way of life”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin diffāmātōrius.

parole.significato: director; directing (related to the managing of a department or company)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dīrēctīvus. First attested in early 15th c..
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dispōnibilis. By surface analysis, disponer (“to have available”) + -ible.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dīversiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs, “transparent”), from διά (diá, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show, reveal”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).

parole.significato: duchy (a dominion or region ruled by a duke or duchess)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ducātus, from Latin dux.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dūrātiōnem, from Latin dūrō.
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin aequātōrem, based on Latin aequō (“to make equal”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin effectuāre.

parole.significato: to execute, to run (enact or carry out)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin executāre, from exsecūtus, perfect passive participle of exsequor, from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”). Ex- becomes ej- in Spanish orthography. Cognate with Portuguese executar, French exécuter, English execute, Italian eseguire.

parole.significato: to exemplify, to give an example, to serve as an example
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exemplificare, from Latin exemplum (“example”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin emergentia, from Latin emergentem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin empȳreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “inflamed”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).
From Medieval Latin in flagrante [dēlīctō].
Borrowed from Medieval Latin entitātem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδημία (epidēmía).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin epistolarium. By surface analysis, epístola + -ario.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aequivalentia.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“a Slav”), from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos) (or borrowed from the Greek directly), see that entry for more. Doublet of eslavo.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sclērōsis, from Ancient Greek σκλήρωσις (sklḗrōsis).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin exclūsa (“sluice, lock”), originally the feminine singular of Latin exclūsus, perfect passive participle of exclūdō (“to exclude”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin scrīptōrium, from Latin scrīptōrius (“pertaining to writing”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Slavus, from Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. Doublet of esclavo.
From Medieval Latin spatulamancia, from Latin spatula (“shoulder blade”) + -mancia.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stigmatizō, from Byzantine Greek στιγματίζω (stigmatízō), from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “tattoo, mark”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sturiōnem, from Frankish *sturjō, from Proto-Germanic *sturjô (“sturgeon”). Cognate with English sturgeon.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin oesophagus, from Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ex abruptō (“abruptly”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin exhumāre, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin factibilis.
From factor + -ía, or borrowed from Medieval Latin factoria, from Latin factor.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharyngem, from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrilis, from Latin febris.
From Medieval Latin feltrum, from Proto-West Germanic *felt, *filt, ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin fīlāmentum, from Late Latin fīlō (“to spin, draw out in a long line”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin forāneus from Latin forās (“outside”). Doublet of huraño.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frangibilis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frāternālis (“fraternal”), from Latin frāternus (“of or relating to a brother, fraternal”), from frāter (“brother”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frontālis (“frontal”), from Latin frōns.
From Medieval Latin geomantia, from Late Ancient Greek γεωμαντεία (geōmanteía). Equivalent to geo- + -mancia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin graduālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin gravāmen.

Back-formation from Old Spanish greñon, from Medieval Latin grenniōnem, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *grendo- (“mustache, beard”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰren- (“facial hair”). Compare Middle Irish grend, Irish greann.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin, from Latin halōs, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose”), in Ecclesiastical Greek (“heretic”), from αἱρετίζω (hairetízō, “to choose”). Doublet of hereje.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin heterogeneus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs, “of different kinds”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin horārius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos), from ὥρα (hṓra, “any limited time”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īconoclasta, from Ancient Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, “breaker of images”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īconographia, from Ancient Greek εἰκονογραφία (eikonographía), from εἰκών (eikṓn, “image, likeness”).
Borrowed from scholastic Medieval Latin identificāre, from Medieval Latin identicus, from Classical Latin idem (“same”), + Latin faciō. Cognate with English identify.
From Medieval Latin identicus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ignitiōnem (“combustion, ignition”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin illēgālis, from Latin lēgālis corresponding to i- + legal.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin imperceptibilis. By surface analysis, im- + perceptible.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin importantia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus.
Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin inclusive, see inclusive.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclūsīvus, from Latin inclūsus.
From Medieval Latin incorruptibilitātem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin incriminare, from Latin criminare.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inductor, from Latin inducō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin inerrantia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnfrangibilis.
From Medieval Latin ingestiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnstantāneus, from Latin īnstantem + -āneus. See Italian istantanea.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnstantāneus, from Latin īnstantem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer (“entire”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intēnsīvus, from Latin intēnsus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intimidāre (“to make afraid”), from Latin in (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”).
From tóxico, or borrowed from Medieval Latin intoxicāre, from Late Latin toxicāre, from Latin toxicus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intrūsus, perfect passive participle of intrūdō, from Latin in- + trūdō (“to thrust”).
From earlier hierarquía, from Medieval Latin hierarchia, from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía) "rule of a high priest", from ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs) "sacred ruler, high priest".

From Medieval Latin syringa, based on Latin syrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, tube”) (genitive singular σῦριγγος (sûringos). The initial consonant must have passed from /s/ to /ʃ/, a sporadic sound change in Old Spanish (compare jabón).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin iūrista.

parole.significato: lip; labial (of or relating to the lips)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin labiālis.

parole.significato: to speak Latin; to write in Latin
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin latināre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin lēctiōnārium. By surface analysis, lección + -ario.
From legítimo + -ar, or borrowed from Medieval Latin legitimāre, from Latin lēgitimus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lenticulāris.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin linguālis, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin logisticus, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós).
From Medieval Latin lupulus.
From Medieval Latin maleficio.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin malvaviscus, from Latin malva (“mallow”) + hibiscum (“marsh mallow”), from Ancient Greek ἱβίσκος (hibískos). Cognate with English mallow, mauve, hibiscus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin manū scrīptus (literally “(thing) written by hand”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin marchasita, from Arabic مَرْقَشِيتَا (marqašītā), while the form margajita is directly from Arabic مَرْقَشِيتَا (marqašītā).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin marcus, from Frankish *marku (“boundary, border”), from Proto-Germanic *markō.

parole.significato: marco, Spanish mark (a traditional unit of weight, equivalent to about 230 g)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin marcus, from Frankish *mark (“mark, sign”), from Proto-Germanic *marką. As a German currency, a calque of German Mark. As a Finnish currency, a calque of Finnish markka, via Old Swedish mark. Cognate with English mark, Catalan marc, and Galician and Portuguese marco.
From Medieval Latin masculīnitās.

parole.significato: to clarify a concept, to be more specific
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin matizare, from Byzantine Greek λαμματίζειν (lammatízein), from λάμμα (lámma) (for λῶμα (lôma, “band, trimming, edge”)).
From older mayorana, majorana, from Medieval Latin maiorana, q.v. (compare French marjolaine, Italian maggiorana, Portuguese manjerona and Sicilian majurana).

parole.significato: merino (relating to the sheep or wool)
parole.testo: Inherited from Medieval Latin maiōrīnus, from maiōr. Cognate with Portuguese meirinho.
From Spanish mesta (“ownerless beast”), from Medieval Latin animālia mixta (“assorted animals”), from Latin mixtus (“mixed”).

parole.significato: metaphysics (branch of philosophy that studies first principles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin metaphysica, methephisica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká). See English metaphysics for further etymology.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin meteōrum, in use as a noun from the neuter of Latin meteōrus, from Ancient Greek μετέωρος (metéōros, “lofty”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin myrtillus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin misericordiōsus. By surface analysis, misericordia + -oso.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin monogamus, from Ancient Greek μονόγαμος (monógamos, “marrying only once”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin morganāticus, from Late Latin mātrimōnium ad morganāticam, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning-gift”), from *murginaz (“morning”) + *gēbǭ (“gift”).
Apparent modification of Medieval Latin mortuārium, based on Latin mortuus (“dead”), from morior (“to die”).

parole.significato: movement (physical motion between points in space)
parole.testo: From mover + -miento, or perhaps partly based on Medieval Latin mōvimentum, from Latin moveō. Cognate with Catalan moviment, Galician movemento, French mouvement, Portuguese movimento.

parole.significato: muscular (of, relating to, or connected with muscles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin or New Latin mūsculāris.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin maxima.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin necessitō (“to oblige, compel”), from Latin necessitās (“necessity, compulsion”) + -ō (denomimal verbal suffix). According to Coromines and Pascual, attested by the 17th century. Cognate of French nécessiter, which is known to be attested much earlier.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nenuphar, from Arabic نِيلَوْفَر (nīlawfar), from Middle Persian nylw(k)pl (/⁠nīlōpal⁠/, “lotus, water-lily”), from Sanskrit नीलोत्पल (nīlotpala, “blue lotus”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nōtōrius (“famous, notorious”), from Late Latin nōtōrius (“pointing out, making known”), from Latin nōtōria (“notice, news”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).
Derived from Medieval Latin numericus.
From Medieval Latin numerus Arabicus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin oda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “poem intended to be sung”), an Attic contraction of ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”).
From Medieval Latin offēnsivus, from Latin offendere (“to offend”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin offēnsīvus, from Latin offēnsus, past participle of offendō (“to offend”). By surface analysis, ofenso + -ivo.
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin offerenda, from Latin offerendus. Compare French offrande, Catalan ofrena, Portuguese oferenda.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesentia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from omni- (“all”) + scientia (“knowledge”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omniscientem (“all-knowing”), from omni (“all”) + sciēns (“knowing”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin onagra, from Ancient Greek ὀνάγρα (onágra).
From Medieval Latin ordālium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ostēnsibilis.
From paliar (“to palliate”) + -t- (“-ive”) + -ivo, from Medieval Latin palliāre (“to cloak”), from Latin pallium (“a cloak”).

parole.significato: tambourine (percussion instrument consisting of a small hoop closed on one side with a drum frame and featuring jinglin…
parole.testo: From Old Spanish pandero, from at least early Medieval Latin pandōrium (“piped instrument”), after Pan, according to Isidore of Seville, from Ancient Greek Πάν (Pán). Writing in thirteenth century Iberia, Juan Gil de Zamora, closely following Isidore but altering the passage, describes it as an inst
Borrowed from Medieval Latin papālis, from Ecclesiastical Latin papa.
Inherited from Old Spanish papadgo, from Medieval Latin papāticus, equivalent to papa (“pope”) + -azgo.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin partiālitātem, from Latin pars.

parole.significato: paroxysm (a random or sudden outburst of activity)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paroxysmus, from Ancient Greek παροξυσμός (paroxusmós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin partītīvus, from Latin partītus + -īvus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin peccābilis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin peccaminōsus (“sinful”), from Late Latin peccāmen (“fault, sin”), from Latin peccō (“to sin”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pediluvium, from pēs (“foot”) and luō (“to wash”).
From Medieval Latin perdūrābilis.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin petrificāre (“to petrify”), from the compounding of petra (“stone, rock”) and -ficō, a suffix from faciō (“to make”). The term petra is from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”); further etymology unknown.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin petroleum, from Latin petra + oleum.
From Medieval Latin pyramidalis. By surface analysis, pirámide + al.
Inherited from Old Spanish plegaria, pregaria (the latter attested in Berceo), semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem.
Ultimately from Medieval Latin placitum. Cognate with Portuguese pleito and English plea.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin plēthōricus, from Ancient Greek πληθωρικός (plēthōrikós).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin plantula.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin portābilis; equivalent to portar + -able.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin portātilis, from Latin portātus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin postergāre, from Latin post (“after”) + tergum (“back, back side”).

parole.significato: to prostrate, lie prostrate, to lie low
parole.testo: Dissimilated from Old Spanish prostrar (e.g. prostrado in Gonzalo de Berceo, 13th century), a borrowing from Medieval Latin prōstrāre, backformed from prōstrātus, perfect passive participle of prōsternō (“to prostrate, to throw down”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin potentiālitātem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedicāmentum, derived from Latin praedicō (“to declare, proclame, predicate”).
From Medieval Latin praelātus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praelūdium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praesuppōnere.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from Late Latin praeambulō.
From Medieval Latin primatia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prīmōgenitūra. By surface analysis, primogénito + -ura.
From Medieval Latin prioritātem.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin prognōsticō, from prognōsticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from προ- (pro-) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “of or for knowing, good at knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to learn, know, perceive, mark, learn”).

From Medieval Latin prognosticum, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from πρό (pró) + γνωστῐκός (gnōstĭkós, “of or for knowing, good at knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to learn to know, to perceive, to mark, to learn”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin propīna, from Latin propinō (“to toast, to pledge, to offer to drink, to hand over”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōpulsiōnem, from Latin prōpulsus. Cognate with English propulsion.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prostata, from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one standing before, protector”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuālis, from punctus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuāre (“to mark with a point, to prick”).

parole.significato: quintal (an unofficial metric unit of mass equal to exactly 100 kg)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin quintāle (“various medieval hundredweights”), from Andalusian Arabic and Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār, “100 rottols”), from Classical Syriac ܩܰܢܛܺܝܪܳܐ (qanṭīrā) and ܩܰܢܛܺܝܢܳܪܳܐ (qanṭīnārā), from Byzantine Greek κεντηνάριον (kentēnárion), from Latin centēnārium (“100 Roman pou

parole.motivo_incerta: Probably; or from; modificatore <unc> nel legame
parole.significato: to remove, to take away, to take down, to take off, to pull off, to pull out, to clear, to clear away, to strip, to str…
parole.testo: Probably a semi-learned derivation from Medieval Latin quitāre (“release, discharge, set free”) from Late Latin quietāre, or from Latin quietus (through an Old Spanish adjective quito, with an abnormal phonological evolution). Compare English quiet and quit and French quitter. See also Spanish queda
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ramificare (“to branch, ramify”), from Latin rāmus (“a branch”) + faciō (“do, make”). Equivalent to ramo + -ificar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ratificāre, from Latin ratus (“established, authoritative; fixed, certain”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin reāctiōnem. By surface analysis, re- + acción.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin receptivus, from Latin receptus.
Derived from Medieval Latin recommendāre, from re- + commendāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin rectangulum.
From Medieval Latin regentia, from Latin regēns, present participle of regō. By surface analysis, regir + -encia.

From Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerere (“to record, to carry back”), from re- + gerere (“to carry, bear”). Compare Latin registoria (“a treasurer”). Some senses influenced by association with unrelated Latin regere (“to rule”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin renegāre, from Latin re- + negō (“to deny”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin reprēnsālia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin residentia, from Latin residēns (“residing”), from resideō (“to reside”), from re- + sedeō (“to sit”).
From Medieval Latin respectivus, from Latin respectus (compare respeto).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin retentīvus, from Latin retentus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin retorta, from Latin retortus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rotātōrius, from Classical Latin rotō. Cognate to Catalan rotatori, French rotatoire, Portuguese rotatório.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin sacristānus, from sacrista (“servant of god, member of a religious community in charge of vestments, ornaments and vessels”), from Latin sacrī (“sacred”) + Late Latin -ista, from Ancient Greek -ιστής (-istḗs).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin saphena, from Arabic صَافِن (ṣāfin), from Hebrew צֹפֵן (ṣōfēn, “hiding”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sanctōrāle.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sebesten, from Arabic سِبِسْتَان (sibistān), from Persian سگپستان (sag-pestân, literally “dog teat”), from سگ (sag, “dog”) + پستان (pestân, “teat”).

parole.significato: secretary (person keeping records and handling clerical work)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sectārius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēdātivus, from Latin sēdātus, perfect passive participle of sēdō.
From Medieval Latin seraphicus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sigla, a feminine singular reinterpreted from a neuter plural of Late Latin siglum (“abbreviation”).
From the Medieval Latin simplificārī.
From Medieval Latin Sina (“China”), from Latin Sinae (“the Southern Chinese; Southern China”), from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v.
Inherited from Old Spanish sobrepelliça (c. 1140), partial calque of Medieval Latin superpellīcium (compare Old French surpeliz), from Latin super (“over”) and pellis (“fur”).
From archaic socarro, from Medieval Latin iocarius (“jester”), from iocus (“joke”).
From Medieval Latin sortilegium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin subōrdināre, from Latin sub- + ōrdinō (“to sort, to order”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin subsūmere, from sub- + sūmō (“take”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin subterfugium, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugio (“to flee”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Suecus, ultimately from Latin Suiōnēs (“Swedes”) (in Tacitus); cognate with Old English Swēon (“Swedes”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin summandus (“to be added”), gerundive of summō (“to add up, to sum”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin summāre (“to add up”), from Latin summa (“sum”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin superioritātem, from Latin superior. By surface analysis, superior + -idad.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin suspēnsōrius (literally “suitable for hanging; sling”), from Latin suspēnsus, perfect passive participle of suspendō (“to hang, to suspend”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin subtīlīzare, from Latin subtīlis. By surface analysis, sutil + -izar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sequitus (“retinue, escort”), from Old Italian seguito (“retinue, entourage, followers”), past participle of seguire (“to follow”), from Latin sequor (“to follow”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tara, from Andalusian Arabic طَرْحَة (ṭarḥa, “that which is thrown away”), a derivative of Arabic طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “to throw (away)”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin tarantula (“wolf spider”), from Italian tarantola, from Taranto (“Taranto (city in Italy where wolf spiders are frequently found)”), from Latin Tarentum, from Ancient Greek Τάρας (Táras) (genitive singular Τάραντος (Tárantos)), possibly from Illyrian *darandos (“oak”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós).

parole.significato: key, button (on a machine or instrument)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin thēcula, diminutive of Latin thēca (“box”), perhaps blended with a descendant of Latin tēgula (“tile”).

Borrowing from Medieval Latin tēnesmus, from Ancient Greek τεινεσμός (teinesmós, “vain endeavor to evacuate”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch, to pull tight”) + -εσμός (-esmós, nominal suffix). First attested in the form tenasmon in 1450, while the form tenesmo appeared in the late 16th c., becoming
Borrowed from Medieval Latin terraqueus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin testimōniāre (“to bear witness, to attest”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin textus (“text”), from Latin textus (“woven”), perfect passive participle of texō (“weave”).
Derived from Medieval Latin tichi michi, variant of tibi mihi "for you, for me", a common expression in petty disputes.
From Medieval Latin thōrācicus, from Ancient Greek θωρᾱκικός (thōrākikós, “suffering in the chest, of the thorax”), from θώραξ (thṓrax, “thorax”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tōtālis, from Latin tōtus + -ālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tractiōnem, from Latin tractus.
From transparente + -encia, or borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentia, from trānspārēns (“transparent”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin transpārentem (“transparent”), from transpareō, from Latin trans + pareō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspirātiōnem, from transpiro, from Latin trāns + spiro.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspirāre, from Latin trāns + spiro.
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trānsubstantiāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānsversālis, from Latin trānsversus.

parole.significato: rag, piece of cloth used for cleaning, washing or drying (tea towel, dish towel, dish cloth, dust cloth, paper towel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin drappus (“cloth”) (via Medieval Latin trapus), probably from Frankish *drapi, *drāpi (“that which is fulled, drabcloth”). Compare French drap, drapeau.
From Medieval Latin triforium.

First used in the 14th century, from Old Spanish trocar, from Medieval Latin trocāre; further etymology uncertain (probably Frankish *trokōn). Cognate with Portuguese, Galician, Catalan, and Occitan trocar, French troquer, English truck.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trachea, from Late Latin trachīa, from Ancient Greek τραχεῖα ἀρτηρία (trakheîa artēría, “rough artery”).

From Medieval Latin or Late Latin theodiscus, Thiotiscus, Teutiscus, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, possibly through an old Italian intermediate, or influenced by it. Cf. French tudesque, Italian tedesco.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ubicātiōnem. First attested in 1630.
From Medieval Latin ubiquitās, from ubīque (“everywhere”).
Inherited from Old Spanish universidat, borrowed from Medieval Latin universitātem. By surface analysis, universo + -idad.

From Medieval Latin vāna glōria, from Latin vāna (“empty, groundless, boastful”) + glōria (“fame, ambition, boasting”). By surface analysis, vana (“vain; arrogant”) + gloria (“glory”). Cognate with English vainglory, Portuguese vanglória and Italian vanagloria.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin veneria, from Latin Venus. Doublet of vieira.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vērificāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin versiōnem (“a turning”).

parole.significato: villancico (traditional Spanish or Portuguese folk song)
parole.testo: From villano (“peasant”), from Medieval Latin vīllānus (“villager”).

parole.significato: virtual (in effect or essence, not in fact or reality)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin virtuālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin volitiōnem, based on Latin volō (“to want”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin volitivus, from volitiō (compare volición), from Latin volō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Scientific Latin jugulāris, previously iugulāris, from Latin iugulum (“neck”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ebanus, from Italian ebano influencing Latin (h)ebenus, ultimately from Egyptian. Doublet of abenuz.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, “a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e., the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from ἐπέχω (epékhō, “to hold in, check”), fr

To be put together with Catalan cofí and French coffin, couffin. Unclear relations. # the Spanish and Catalan have been considered borrowed from Arabic قُفَّة (quffa, “basket”), also present in Spanish cofa, Catalan cofa, Portuguese alcofa, which borrowing would have to be suffixed + -ín; # or they

parole.significato: pair of compasses (tool used to draw circles)
parole.testo: Apparently from Old French compas, perhaps from Medieval Latin compassus (“circle, circuit”), or the medieval Latin term is derived from Old French. In either case, deverbal from Vulgar Latin *compassāre (“to pace off”), from com- + *passāre (“to step”), from Latin passus (“step”), originally the pe

parole.significato: a tile of a board to play chess or checkers
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin scaccum or a corresponding Romance word, e.g. Catalan escac (“check!; chess piece”) and escacs (“chess”), from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “shah; king in chess”) or شَاهُك (šāhuk, “your king”); see related jaque. Cognate with Italian scacco, French échec, Old Occitan escac (“chess
Either derived or related to fieltro, or from Medieval Latin filtrum, from Frankish *filtir, plural of *filt, from Proto-West Germanic *felt (“felt”).

Borrowed from Middle High German trampen (“to walk heavily”), or from Medieval Latin trappa, from Proto-Germanic *trap-, from Proto-Indo-European *dremb- (“to run”); or possibly ultimately onomatopoeic (compare English trap).
